passages.passage_text:
Translators have long been described as traitors, and the accusation rests on an assumption so familiar that it rarely receives scrutiny: that a text possesses a stable core of meaning that exists prior to any language, and that the translator's task is to carry this core across a border without spilling any of it. On this view, a good translation is a transparent window and a bad one is a smudged pane. The metaphor is attractive because it flatters the original, but it conceals more than it reveals.

Consider what a translator of a nineteenth-century novel actually confronts. A sentence may be long, its subordinate clauses stacked like crates, while the target language may prefer short declaratives. To break the sentence is to alter the rhythm that gave the narrator an air of fussy deliberation; to preserve it is to produce English that no reader would call natural. Neither choice is neutral. Fidelity to syntax and fidelity to effect pull in opposite directions, and the translator must decide which to betray. The window metaphor has no place for such a decision, since a window does not choose.

Some theorists have responded by inverting the hierarchy, arguing that translation is a form of authorship and that the translated text is a new work that merely shares a lineage with its source. This position has the virtue of honesty about the translator's labor, but it overcorrects. A translator who feels free to rewrite the plot, relocate the setting, or silence a troublesome character is not exercising creative license so much as abandoning an obligation. Readers who pick up a translation extend a particular kind of trust: they assume that the book in their hands answers to another book, and that its departures, where they occur, are the price of conveying something rather than the product of whim.

A more defensible account treats translation as interpretation, comparable to a pianist's reading of a sonata. No one supposes that two performances of the same sonata must be identical in order for both to be faithful, yet no one supposes that any sequence of notes counts as a performance of it either. The score constrains without determining. Similarly, the source text sets limits, so that some renderings are simply wrong, while leaving a wide field of legitimate variation. Disagreement among translators then appears not as evidence of failure but as the natural consequence of a text rich enough to sustain more than one reading.

This account also explains a curious feature of literary history: translations age faster than originals. A novel written in 1850 may still read as lively prose, while its English version from 1890 strikes us as stiff and quaint. If translation merely transferred a fixed meaning, there would be no reason for the English version to date, since the meaning has not changed. But if a translation is an interpretation shaped by the idiom and expectations of its own moment, then it will inevitably carry the marks of that moment, and later readers will perceive them as the dust of an earlier age. The original, written within the living language, is dated only in the way that all older books are; the translation is dated twice.

None of this implies that retranslation is wasteful. Each generation of translators, by making different compromises, reveals aspects of the source that earlier versions obscured. The proliferation of versions is not a sign that the work has been lost in transit but that it continues to be found.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Translators should be regarded as authors of new works whose obligations to the source are minimal.
options.B: Translation is better understood as a constrained act of interpretation than as the transfer of a fixed meaning between languages.
options.C: Translations inevitably betray their originals, so retranslation is largely wasteful.
options.D: Nineteenth-century novels are especially hard to translate because of their long sentences.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) This captures the author's rejection of the window metaphor and endorsement of the pianist analogy. Why the others are wrong: A) The author calls this view an overcorrection. C) The author explicitly denies that retranslation is wasteful. D) The long sentence is only an illustration, not the point of the passage.
questions.trap: Choosing the authorship view because it gets extended discussion; the author presents it as an overcorrection, not as the conclusion.

questions.stem: The author discusses the long, subordinate-clause-heavy sentence primarily to show that

options.A: translators must choose between competing kinds of fidelity, a feature the window metaphor cannot represent.
options.B: readers generally prefer natural-sounding translations to literal ones, so translators should always favor fluency over fidelity
options.C: target languages generally prefer shorter sentences than source languages do, so long sentences are always broken up
options.D: nineteenth-century prose is stylistically inferior to modern prose.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author ties the example to the claim that a window does not choose. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage never reports reader preferences. C) The example is hypothetical and used to illustrate a choice, not a general rule about languages. D) No evaluation of the novel's quality is offered.
questions.trap: Turning an illustrative example into a general claim about languages instead of asking what point it serves in the argument.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the view that translation is a form of authorship is best described as

options.A: qualified approval, crediting one merit while rejecting its extreme conclusion.
options.B: neutral indifference, since the author neither credits nor criticizes the view that translators are authors
options.C: enthusiastic endorsement, treating translators as authors whose duties to the source text are minimal
options.D: dismissive contempt, treating the view as having no merit whatsoever for the understanding of translation

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author praises its honesty about the translator's labor but says it overcorrects. Why the others are wrong: B) The author takes a clear evaluative stance. C) The author says the view overcorrects and abandons an obligation. D) The author grants that the view has a virtue.
questions.trap: Reading a sentence of praise as the author's overall position and ignoring the 'but it overcorrects' that follows.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a translation is 'dated twice' because

options.A: translators of earlier eras were less skilled than modern translators, so their versions now seem clumsy and outdated
options.B: the source language changes faster than the target language, leaving the original harder to read with each decade
options.C: the meaning of the source text changes over time while the translation stays fixed in the words of its own period
options.D: it ages as an older book and also bears the idiom and expectations of the period in which it was made.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The passage gives exactly these two sources of datedness. Why the others are wrong: A) Skill is never discussed as a cause. B) The passage makes no comparison of rates of linguistic change. C) The passage says the meaning has not changed.
questions.trap: Supplying a plausible outside explanation (translator skill) rather than the one the passage actually states.

questions.stem: Two respected translators render a poem very differently, but one mistakes a word meaning 'river bank' for one meaning 'financial institution.' Based on the passage, the author would most likely say that

options.A: both renderings are equally legitimate because disagreement among respected translators is natural and the source permits many readings
options.B: the stylistic difference is an error, but the mistaken word is acceptable creative license because translators are authors in their own right
options.C: the stylistic difference reflects legitimate variation, while the mistaken word falls outside the limits the source sets.
options.D: both renderings are failures because neither matches the original exactly and no translation could ever meet that standard

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author says the source constrains without determining, so some renderings are simply wrong. Why the others are wrong: A) The author states that some renderings are simply wrong. B) This reverses the author's position. D) The author rejects exact transfer as the standard.
questions.trap: Over-applying 'disagreement is natural' to every difference, forgetting the limits the source text still sets.

questions.stem: The passage attributes which of the following assumptions to those who call translators traitors?

options.A: Readers who lack the source language cannot judge whether a translation is accurate, so they must simply trust the translator.
options.B: A text has a meaning that exists independently of any language and can be carried over intact.
options.C: A translation should sound more natural to its readers than the original sounded to its first audience.
options.D: Translators generally lack sufficient knowledge of the source language to render its subtler meanings reliably.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) This is the 'stable core of meaning' in the first paragraph. Why the others are wrong: A) No claim about readers' judgment is attributed to the accusers. C) The passage says naturalness and fidelity can conflict, not that traitors want naturalness. D) Competence is never mentioned.
questions.trap: Picking a statement that sounds like a reason to call translators traitors without checking it against the passage's first paragraph.

passages.passage_text:
City planners have traditionally regarded street vending as a symptom of disorder, a residue of underdevelopment that modernization will eventually sweep away. Municipal codes in many cities reflect this assumption: vendors are licensed sparingly, confined to designated zones, or prohibited outright in commercial districts. Yet in cities around the world the number of street vendors has not declined as economies have grown; in several it has risen. This persistence is awkward for the view that vending is a transitional phenomenon, and it has prompted researchers to ask whether the planners' premise was mistaken from the start.

One line of argument holds that vending persists because it performs functions that formal retail does not. A vendor stationed outside a transit station sells to commuters at precisely the moment and place where demand peaks, in quantities as small as a single piece of fruit or a pair of batteries. Large stores cannot profitably serve such demand, because their costs of rent, staffing, and inventory presuppose bulk sales and steady foot traffic. The vendor's low overhead is not a defect of the enterprise but the source of its flexibility. Moreover, vending offers entry to people excluded from formal employment by lack of credentials, capital, or documentation. To close the street is therefore not simply to remove an eyesore; it is to remove a rung from a ladder that some residents have no other way of climbing.

Critics of vending respond that these virtues are purchased at a cost borne by others. Crowded sidewalks impede pedestrians, particularly those with disabilities; uninspected food poses health risks; and vendors who pay no taxes enjoy an advantage over shopkeepers who do. These objections deserve to be taken seriously, but they are not all of one kind. Some concern genuine harms, such as obstruction and contamination, which can in principle be addressed through regulation of where and how vending occurs. Others concern fairness among competitors, which might be addressed by bringing vendors into the tax system on terms they can afford. Only if one assumes that vending cannot be regulated, and can only be tolerated or eliminated, does the existence of these costs justify prohibition.

The experience of cities that have tried regulation is instructive but mixed. Where authorities have negotiated with vendor associations over designated spaces, standardized stalls, and modest fees, congestion has often fallen and complaints have diminished. But in other cities, formalization has produced fees and permit requirements that only the more established vendors could meet, driving the poorest out to operate illegally and thereby exposing them to harassment and confiscation. The lesson is not that regulation fails but that its design matters: rules written without the participation of those they govern tend to serve the interests of those who wrote them.

It would be a mistake, then, to treat the debate as a contest between order and chaos. The street is a shared resource whose uses compete, and every arrangement of it, including the arrangement that excludes vendors, embodies a judgment about whose needs count. Planners who recognize this are better placed to ask which combination of rules would allow pedestrians, shopkeepers, and vendors to coexist, rather than assuming that one of the three is an intruder.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Vendors' advantages over shopkeepers, such as lower rent and exemption from taxes, are unfair enough to justify prohibiting street vending outright.
options.B: Street vending persists for reasons planners overlooked, so the productive question is how to design fair regulations rather than whether to eliminate it.
options.C: Street vending is a transitional phenomenon that will fade on its own as cities grow richer and formal retail expands, so no policy response is needed.
options.D: Cities that regulate vending have consistently reduced congestion and complaints, which shows that regulation works better than tolerance or prohibition.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) This combines the persistence argument with the closing call for well-designed rules. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says fairness concerns can be addressed by other means. C) The passage cites rising vendor numbers against this view. D) The passage calls the evidence mixed.
questions.trap: Choosing an extreme position (ban or celebrate) when the author consistently takes the middle, design-focused position.

questions.stem: The author mentions a single piece of fruit and a pair of batteries in order to

options.A: argue that small purchases are economically unimportant and therefore not worth regulating or counting.
options.B: show that vendors depend on commuters more than on any other customers, since commuters buy in small quantities.
options.C: suggest that vendors' goods are of lower quality than those sold in stores, which explains their lower prices.
options.D: illustrate demand that formal stores cannot profitably serve given their cost structures.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The next sentence explains that large stores' costs presuppose bulk sales. Why the others are wrong: A) The author uses them to show vending's value. B) The example illustrates quantity, not customer dependence. C) Quality is never compared.
questions.trap: Reading the examples as trivial items rather than as evidence of small-quantity demand.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the costs critics attribute to vending would justify prohibition only if

options.A: formal retailers could not otherwise compete with vendors who avoid rents, licenses, and taxes.
options.B: pedestrian obstruction outweighed the benefits that vending provides to commuters and low-income buyers.
options.C: vending could not be regulated and could only be tolerated or eliminated.
options.D: vendors refused to pay any taxes even when offered a workable way to do so.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author states this condition directly in the third paragraph. Why the others are wrong: A) Competition is treated as a fairness issue, not a condition for prohibition. B) No such weighing is described. D) The author suggests bringing vendors into the tax system.
questions.trap: Choosing an option that restates a critic's complaint instead of the condition the author names.

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the argument that vending persists because it fills roles formal retail does not?

options.A: Vendor numbers are highest near transit stations and other places where large crowds gather at predictable hours of the day.
options.B: Many vendors lack formal credentials or documentation that would qualify them for work in the formal retail sector, which is closed to them.
options.C: Most vendor sales are of the same products, in the same quantities and at the same prices as those at nearby formal stores.
options.D: Vendors' overhead is much lower than the rent, utilities, and licensing fees paid by formal stores selling comparable goods.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) This implies vendors are not filling a distinct role. Why the others are wrong: A) This fits the argument about peak demand at particular places. B) This supports the claim that vending offers entry to the excluded. D) This supports the flexibility argument.
questions.trap: Selecting a fact that sounds negative about vendors but actually fits the argument being tested.

questions.stem: The author's treatment of the critics' objections can best be described as

options.A: dismissive, treating the objections as pretexts for excluding the poor from public space entirely.
options.B: resigned, accepting that the costs of vending cannot be reduced by any regulatory design.
options.C: alarmed, because the harms to pedestrians and shopkeepers are described as severe and growing.
options.D: even-handed, granting their seriousness while distinguishing among them.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author says they deserve to be taken seriously and then sorts them into two kinds. Why the others are wrong: A) The author does not question the critics' motives. B) The author argues regulation can address them. C) The tone is analytical rather than alarmed.
questions.trap: Equating a pro-vendor argument with hostility toward the critics.

questions.stem: A city that wished to follow the passage's closing advice would most likely

options.A: set a fee schedule through city officials alone and enforce it strictly with fines and confiscation of goods from violators.
options.B: convene vendors, shopkeepers, and pedestrian representatives to draft rules for sharing sidewalk space.
options.C: move vendors out of commercial districts to designated peripheral zones where they would not obstruct pedestrians or compete with stores.
options.D: stop regulating vending entirely and leave the use of sidewalk space to be settled by individual vendors and shopkeepers.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) This reflects the idea that rules should be shaped with those they govern and that none of the three is an intruder. Why the others are wrong: A) The author warns against rules written without participation. C) This treats vendors as intruders. D) The author favors well-designed regulation, not none.
questions.trap: Mistaking opposition to prohibition for opposition to any regulation.

passages.passage_text:
When photography became widely available in the nineteenth century, many commentators greeted it as a machine for preserving the past. A photograph seemed to hold a moment in suspension, immune to the fading and embellishment that corrupt the memories of those who were present. Families commissioned portraits of the dying; governments documented monuments; travelers returned with images of places their neighbors would never see. The camera, it was said, could not lie, and a civilization that possessed it would never again lose its history.

The confidence was misplaced, and the reasons are more interesting than the usual complaint that images can be manipulated. Even an unaltered photograph records a decision. Someone chose the angle, the framing, the moment, and, just as important, what to leave outside the frame. A photograph of a harvest festival may omit the debts that burdened the farmers; a photograph of a factory may show gleaming machinery and no workers. The image is accurate in what it shows and silent about what it excludes, and the silence is easily mistaken for absence. Viewers rarely ask what lay a few feet to the left. A caption adds a further layer of selection, since the words beneath an image tell viewers what to notice and what to ignore.

A subtler difficulty concerns what photographs do to the memories they were meant to protect. Psychologists have long observed that remembering is not retrieval of a stored record but reconstruction, assembled anew each time from fragments and expectations. When a photograph is available, it supplies the fragments. Over years, a person who looks repeatedly at an image of a childhood birthday may come to remember the party as the photograph depicts it, with the remembered scene acquiring the photograph's composition, its vantage point, even its colors. Events that were never photographed, meanwhile, receive no such reinforcement and may fade. The camera, in other words, does not merely preserve the past; it selects the portions of it that will survive in memory, and it does so according to what was photographed rather than what mattered.

This selective effect has consequences that extend beyond the individual. Societies, like persons, remember through the artifacts they have. An archive heavy with images of official ceremonies and light on images of ordinary labor will tend to yield a history of ceremonies. Those who were rarely photographed, because they lacked the means or the standing to commission portraits, are underrepresented in the visual record and thus easier to forget. Photography, which was supposed to democratize memory, has in many periods reproduced the hierarchies of the societies that practiced it.

None of this is an argument for discarding photographs. The remedy for a partial record is a larger and more varied one, together with a habit of reading images as evidence produced by particular people for particular purposes. A photograph read in this way becomes more informative, not less, because its omissions, once noticed, are themselves data. What is required is a shift in how we regard the medium: not as a mirror held up to the past, but as one witness among many in a continuing argument about it.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Early commentators were right that photography democratized historical memory.
options.B: Photography has damaged memory so much that archives should avoid relying on it.
options.C: Photographs, though once thought to preserve the past faithfully, are selective records that also shape memory and should be read critically alongside other evidence.
options.D: Photographs are unreliable chiefly because they can be manipulated.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) This covers selection, memory, and the closing recommendation. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says it often reproduced hierarchies. B) The author says photographs should not be discarded. D) The author sets aside manipulation as the 'usual complaint'.
questions.trap: Selecting the familiar complaint (manipulation) that the author explicitly moves beyond.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a person who repeatedly views a photograph of a childhood event may

options.A: come to remember the event with the photograph's composition and vantage point.
options.B: forget the event entirely once the photograph has replaced the original experience in memory.
options.C: recall the event more accurately than someone who has never seen the photograph, because the image fixes the details.
options.D: come to distrust the photograph because it conflicts with the person's own recollection of the day.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The third paragraph says the remembered scene acquires the photograph's features. Why the others are wrong: B) It is the unphotographed events that may fade. C) The passage says the memory is reshaped, not made more accurate. D) No such reaction is described.
questions.trap: Assuming that reinforcement by a photograph means a more accurate memory.

questions.stem: The author mentions a harvest festival and a factory in order to illustrate that

options.A: images of labor are more valuable to later historians than images of ceremonies and public celebrations.
options.B: an accurate photograph can still mislead through what it leaves out.
options.C: photographers deliberately conceal economic hardship in order to flatter the powerful people who hired them.
options.D: governments commissioned most early photographs in order to promote official accounts of local life.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Both examples show a true image that is silent about debts or workers. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage does not rank image types by value in these examples. C) The passage describes silence, not deliberate concealment. D) The examples are not about who commissioned images.
questions.trap: Attributing intent to photographers where the passage only describes what a frame excludes.

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim about how photographs affect memory?

options.A: Participants who repeatedly viewed photographs of an event later recalled it no differently from those who never saw them.
options.B: Participants who viewed photographs reported greater confidence in their memories of the event, though their accounts were no more detailed.
options.C: Participants shown a photograph afterward described the event using details that were present in the photograph and absent from other accounts.
options.D: Events that were never photographed were recalled less often and less vividly than photographed ones, even after controlling for importance.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) This directly contradicts the claim that photographs reshape recollection. Why the others are wrong: B) Confidence is not accuracy or content, so this neither weakens nor clearly supports. C) This supports the claim. D) This supports the claim about selective survival.
questions.trap: Choosing a finding about confidence, which is not the same as the content or accuracy of memory.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the nineteenth-century belief that the camera could not lie is best described as

options.A: uncertain, offering no judgment of it because the evidence is too sparse for a verdict.
options.B: admiring of its optimism, since it expressed hope that images could democratize knowledge.
options.C: scornful of those who held it, regarding them as naive about the new technology.
options.D: critical, though attentive to why the belief seemed reasonable.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author calls the confidence misplaced yet describes why people held it. Why the others are wrong: A) The author states a clear judgment. B) The author says the confidence was misplaced. C) The author's tone toward early commentators is not contemptuous.
questions.trap: Confusing criticism of an idea with scorn for the people who held it.

questions.stem: A historian using a town's photographic archive from 1900 would, following the author's advice, most likely

options.A: treat the images as the most reliable evidence available because they are unaltered records of exactly what was there at the time.
options.B: discard the archive because it overrepresents town officials and the wealthy residents who paid for portraits and public ceremonies.
options.C: rely on residents' memories instead of the photographs because memories are free of the camera's selective and posed view of the town.
options.D: ask who made the photographs and for what purpose, note what is absent, and supplement them with other sources.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) This reflects reading images as evidence produced for particular purposes with omissions as data. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says unaltered images still record decisions. B) The author says not to discard photographs. C) Memories are also reconstructed, according to the passage.
questions.trap: Overcorrecting from naive trust to complete rejection.

passages.passage_text:
Before the late nineteenth century, most towns kept their own time. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest overhead, and clocks in neighboring towns might differ by several minutes without anyone being troubled. The arrangement worked because few people needed to coordinate with anyone beyond walking distance. The railroad changed this. A train traveling between distant cities crossed many local times in a single journey, and timetables listing arrivals according to a dozen different noons were nearly useless. Railway companies therefore adopted standard time zones, and within a generation most communities had set their clocks to match.

The usual account treats this change as a triumph of practicality, a case of technology demanding rationality and rationality obliging. There is truth in this, but the account leaves out the resistance. Many towns resisted the new time, regarding it as an imposition by distant corporations on local custom. Newspaper editors complained that the railroads had presumed to alter the day itself. Some communities maintained two sets of time, one for the railway station and one for everything else, and a few clung to local time for years. That the resistance eventually faded reveals less about the persuasiveness of the arguments than about the mounting costs of standing apart: a town that kept its own time could not be conveniently reached, and so it gradually lost the commerce that depended on being reachable.

Sociologists have drawn from this episode a broader lesson about how standards spread. A standard is valuable largely because others use it, and its value to any single adopter increases with the number of adopters. Such arrangements tend to be unstable in the early period, when no one wishes to be first, and then abruptly self-reinforcing once a critical mass has been reached. Once most had adopted railway time, holdouts faced pressure not from the railways' power but from the choices of their neighbors, who preferred to deal with those whose clocks agreed with their own.

The adoption of standard time also altered how people experienced the day. When time was local and tied to the sun, it was understood as a feature of the natural world, something observed rather than set. Standard time was visibly conventional: it could be adjusted by agreement, and it applied equally to a place where the sun had risen and one where it had not. As clock time grew detached from the sun, it became easier to treat as a resource to be measured, scheduled, and allocated. Factory managers could compare hours worked; schools could divide the day into uniform periods; workers began to speak of being "on the clock." Whether these developments flowed from standard time or merely coincided with it is difficult to establish, since industrialization was proceeding for independent reasons. But the timing suggests that a shared, conventional time made certain habits of mind easier to acquire.

It would be wrong to conclude that the change was simply imposed on a passive public, or that it was freely chosen. The more accurate description lies between: individuals made rational choices, but the range of choices available to them was determined by decisions others had already made.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the passage?

options.A: The adoption of standard time was neither simple imposition nor free choice but resulted from choices constrained by others' earlier decisions, and it may have encouraged new habits of mind.
options.B: Standard time caused the scheduling habits of industrial society.
options.C: Standard time spread because communities recognized it as more rational.
options.D: Railway companies imposed standard time on communities that had no power to resist.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) This captures the resistance, the standards lesson, and the closing synthesis. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says causation is hard to establish. C) The author says the usual account of rational obliging leaves out resistance. D) The passage describes resistance and neighbors' pressure, not direct imposition.
questions.trap: Choosing a single-cause explanation after the author rejects both single-cause accounts.

questions.stem: According to the passage, local resistance to standard time faded mainly because

options.A: the arguments for standard time proved persuasive to local officials and ordinary residents alike.
options.B: railway companies directly punished towns that kept local time by withholding service and freight.
options.C: standing apart made a town harder to reach and cost it commerce.
options.D: newspaper editors changed their positions and began urging readers to adopt the new time.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The second paragraph attributes the fading to the mounting costs of standing apart. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says the fading reveals less about persuasiveness. B) The pressure came from neighbors' choices, not railway power. D) No such change is reported.
questions.trap: Selecting the 'persuasion' answer that matches the usual account the author is criticizing.

questions.stem: The detail that some communities kept two sets of time serves to

options.A: suggest that dual timekeeping was a stable long-term solution.
options.B: show that railway time was less accurate than local time.
options.C: illustrate the extent of the resistance to standard time.
options.D: demonstrate that local time was more reliable.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) It appears among the examples of resistance. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says resistance eventually faded. B) Accuracy is not at issue. D) No reliability comparison is made.
questions.trap: Reading a detail as evidence for a claim the passage never makes.

questions.stem: Which situation is most analogous to the spread of standards described in the third paragraph?

options.A: A factory buys a new machine because it lowers costs of production, whatever other factories decide to do.
options.B: A messaging app grows more useful to each person as more friends join, so holdouts eventually sign up.
options.C: A restaurant grows popular after a single critic's favorable review appears in the local newspaper and draws steady crowds.
options.D: A government mandates a new currency and punishes anyone who continues to use the old one in trade.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Value rises with the number of adopters and holdouts follow their neighbors. Why the others are wrong: A) The benefit does not depend on others' adoption. C) This involves no increasing value to each adopter. D) The passage stresses neighbors' choices rather than coercive power.
questions.trap: Matching on surface features (change of practice) instead of the mechanism of increasing value with adoption.

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the author's suggestion that conventional time made new habits of mind easier to acquire?

options.A: Industrialization proceeded faster in regions with more railways, and those regions also adopted standard time earliest and most completely.
options.B: Regions that kept local time for decades adopted clock-based scheduling in factories and schools as quickly as standard-time regions did.
options.C: Factory managers in standard-time regions began comparing hours worked, output per shift, and wages across different plants.
options.D: Most regions abandoned local time within a generation, and almost none returned to it afterward even when they were free to do so.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) This suggests standard time was not what drove the new habits. Why the others are wrong: A) This is consistent with the independent industrialization the author mentions and does not test the claim. C) This is consistent with the author's claim. D) This concerns adoption speed, not the habits of mind.
questions.trap: Picking a finding that fits the author's own account of coinciding developments.

questions.stem: The final paragraph primarily serves to

options.A: reject a choice between two extreme characterizations of how standard time was adopted.
options.B: assign blame to the railway companies for forcing communities to give up their local time.
options.C: introduce an objection to the sociologists' lesson about how standards spread through neighbors' choices.
options.D: summarize the evidence for resistance to standard time offered in the earlier paragraphs of the passage.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) It says neither pure imposition nor free choice is accurate. Why the others are wrong: B) It describes constraints without assigning blame. C) It builds on rather than objects to the earlier analysis. D) No new summary of evidence appears.
questions.trap: Treating a concluding synthesis as a new argument or a summary.

passages.passage_text:
Listeners who encounter recordings made in the first decades of the twentieth century are often struck by how odd the performances sound. Violinists slide between notes with a persistence that modern players avoid; pianists roll chords and let the hands fall slightly out of synchrony; singers take liberties with tempo that a present-day conductor would not tolerate. The natural reaction is to suppose that these musicians were simply less disciplined than their successors, or that their era had not yet discovered the precision that recording would later demand.

This reaction mistakes a difference in convention for a difference in skill. The performers in question were frequently of extraordinary ability, and their departures from the written score were deliberate. In the tradition they inherited, a score was understood as a sketch rather than a specification; the performer's responsibility was to supply expressive inflection that notation could not capture, and a performance that adhered rigidly to the printed rhythm would have been considered lifeless. The modern ideal, in which the performer's task is to realize the composer's text with minimal intrusion, is itself a historical development, not an eternal standard.

Why did the ideal change? One explanation points to the recording itself. A live performance is heard once, and an idiosyncratic gesture that delights in the moment is forgotten in the next. A recording is heard again and again, and the same gesture, repeated, can begin to grate. Performers who knew their work would be preserved had reason to prefer interpretations that would withstand repetition, and listeners who could compare multiple recordings of the same piece began to notice and prize accuracy. Competition among recordings thus rewarded a kind of precision that concert halls had never demanded.

This explanation is plausible, but it is incomplete. Changes in taste were underway before recording became common, and they were driven partly by composers who grew impatient with what they regarded as performers' liberties. Several prominent composers of the period published increasingly detailed markings and issued public complaints about interpreters who altered their work. The recording industry may have accelerated the shift, but it found a movement already in progress, and it is unlikely to have created it.

There is a further irony. The performers whose styles now seem eccentric left recordings that make it possible to hear what they actually did, and the recordings reveal that written descriptions of their art can be misleading. Critics of the time praised a violinist's "restraint" or a pianist's "fidelity," words that a modern listener, hearing the recordings, would never apply. The vocabulary of praise had meant something different. Without the recordings we would have assumed that earlier musicians played much as we do and that the words meant what they mean to us. The medium that is blamed for standardizing performance has also preserved the evidence that standards were once otherwise.

That evidence invites humility. If conventions that seemed natural to one generation appear strange to the next, we have little reason to believe that our own are exempt from the same fate. Future listeners may find our scrupulous literalism as peculiar as we find the slides and rolled chords of our predecessors.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Recording technology caused performers to abandon expressive freedom in favor of precision.
options.B: Modern performers should revive the slides and rolled chords of earlier players.
options.C: Early recordings sound odd because they reflect older performance conventions rather than lesser skill, and the later turn to literalism had several causes and is itself historically contingent.
options.D: Early performers were less disciplined than modern ones.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) This covers the convention argument, the causes, and the closing humility. Why the others are wrong: A) The author calls this explanation incomplete. B) The author makes no such recommendation. D) The author calls this a mistake of convention for skill.
questions.trap: Choosing the explanation the author presents first and then qualifies.

questions.stem: According to the passage, in the tradition inherited by early twentieth-century performers a score was regarded as

options.A: a guide meant for composers to consult while composing rather than for performers to follow in public.
options.B: a precise specification to be realized without alteration or any expressive addition by the performer.
options.C: a historical document of little practical use to performers beyond establishing the notes.
options.D: an outline to which the performer added expressive inflection.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author calls it a sketch rather than a specification. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage never suggests this. B) This describes the modern ideal. C) The score was still the basis of performance.
questions.trap: Confusing the older convention with the modern ideal the passage contrasts it with.

questions.stem: The author's view of the claim that recording caused the change in performance ideals is that it is

options.A: entirely mistaken, since recording had no effect on performance ideals whatsoever.
options.B: fully adequate to explain the change without reference to any other cause or earlier development.
options.C: plausible but incomplete, because taste was already shifting.
options.D: irrelevant to the history of performance, since technology never affects musical taste.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author states exactly this. Why the others are wrong: A) The author calls the explanation plausible and grants the industry accelerated the shift. B) The author calls it incomplete. D) The author treats it as a real contributing factor.
questions.trap: Reading 'incomplete' as 'wrong' or ignoring the concession in 'plausible.'

questions.stem: The author mentions critics who praised 'restraint' and 'fidelity' in order to show that

options.A: the vocabulary of praise meant something different then, so recordings can correct what written descriptions suggest.
options.B: performers of the time deliberately sought restraint, as the critics' praise indicates to modern listeners of the recordings.
options.C: modern critics misuse words that earlier critics used correctly, so present-day reviews cannot be trusted as guides.
options.D: critics of the time were poorly informed about music and could not hear what performers were actually doing.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author says the words meant something different and that recordings reveal this. Why the others are wrong: B) The recordings show the opposite by modern standards. C) The passage does not blame modern critics. D) The point concerns changing word meanings, not competence.
questions.trap: Assuming the critics were wrong rather than recognizing a shift in meaning.

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that changes in taste preceded the spread of recording?

options.A: Composers' public complaints and detailed markings appeared only after records were widely sold.
options.B: Listeners compared different recordings of the same piece and began to prefer the more literal performances.
options.C: Some performers continued the older style on recordings made well after the new literalism had become common.
options.D: Recordings of the same piece circulated widely by 1920, giving listeners many versions to compare.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) This removes the timing evidence for earlier change. Why the others are wrong: B) This supports the recording explanation, not the timing claim. C) This does not bear on when taste began to shift. D) This is consistent with both accounts.
questions.trap: Choosing a fact that supports the rival (recording) explanation without actually undermining the timing claim.

questions.stem: The final paragraph suggests that the author would most likely agree that

options.A: future listeners will prefer the older style to the modern one once literalism has run its course.
options.B: present-day performance conventions should not be assumed to be the permanent standard of correctness.
options.C: scrupulous literalism is a defect in modern performance that performers should be encouraged to abandon.
options.D: recordings are poor evidence of past practice because performers behaved differently before a microphone.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author warns our own conventions may seem strange to later listeners. Why the others are wrong: A) The author predicts only that they may find our style peculiar. C) The author does not condemn it. D) The author calls recordings valuable evidence.
questions.trap: Turning a call for humility into a verdict against modern practice.

passages.passage_text:
Economists often describe exchange as the trading of goods whose values the parties have compared and found equal enough to make the transaction worthwhile. On this model, a gift is an anomaly: a transfer of value without anything received in return. The standard way of handling the anomaly has been to explain it away, either by treating gifts as disguised self-interest, given to win favor or to be repaid later, or by relegating them to the private sphere of families, where market logic is held not to apply. Anthropologists who have studied societies in which gifts structure much of economic life have argued that both responses miss what gift exchange is for.

In many of these societies, giving creates a relationship rather than settling one. A gift is not equivalent to a payment because it is not meant to close an account. A person who receives a gift acquires an obligation, but the obligation is open-ended: to return something, at some later time, of a kind and amount that cannot be precisely specified. Attempting to repay at once, or with exact equivalence, is understood as an insult, a refusal of the relationship, since it announces that the recipient wishes to owe nothing. The unspecified and deferred quality of the return is not a flaw in the system but its point. Debt that remains outstanding keeps the parties bound to one another.

This analysis helps clarify why gifts and sales feel different even when the objects involved are the same. A commercial transaction is designed to leave the parties independent: after the money changes hands, neither owes the other anything and neither need meet again. A gift is designed to do the opposite. Consider the difference between handing a neighbor cash for a favor and bringing a pie after the neighbor has watched one's house. The cash may be worth more, yet it may seem faintly offensive, because it treats the neighbor as a vendor rather than as someone with whom one expects to remain in a relationship.

It would be a mistake, however, to infer that gift economies are more benevolent than markets. The obligations that bind people can also trap them. A chief who gives lavishly can place rivals under debts they cannot discharge, converting generosity into dominance. In such settings the gift is a weapon as well as a bond, and the person who cannot reciprocate is diminished rather than comforted. The open-ended character of the debt that sustains cooperation also sustains inequality.

Nor are the two systems cleanly separated in modern life. Employers speak of loyalty and offer perquisites that are not strictly wages; merchants cultivate regular customers with small unrequested favors; professionals trade courtesies that no contract requires. Each of these ordinary practices blends the logic of the market with the logic of the gift, and each depends on the ambiguity. When the gift element is made explicit as a calculated inducement, it tends to lose its force, because the recipient recognizes that the relationship being offered is itself being priced.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Modern life has replaced gift exchange with market exchange.
options.B: Gift economies are more benevolent than market economies.
options.C: Gift exchange creates and sustains relationships through open-ended obligation, distinguishing it from market exchange, although it can also sustain hierarchy and blends with market practices today.
options.D: Gifts are disguised self-interest and are best analyzed as market transactions.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) This includes the central claim and the two qualifications. Why the others are wrong: A) The final paragraph says the two remain mixed. B) The fourth paragraph rejects this inference. D) The author says this response misses what gift exchange is for.
questions.trap: Selecting the economists' view that the author sets out to criticize.

questions.stem: According to the passage, immediate repayment in exact equivalence is regarded as an insult in many gift societies because it

options.A: implies that the giver is wealthier than the recipient and therefore expects the recipient to repay more.
options.B: violates a rule against any return of gifts, which would be treated as an insult in itself.
options.C: suggests that the gift was of low value and so can be matched exactly without further obligation.
options.D: signals that the recipient wishes to owe nothing and thus refuses the relationship.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author states this directly. Why the others are wrong: A) Wealth is not mentioned in this context. B) A return is expected, only deferred and unspecified. C) Value is not the issue.
questions.trap: Assuming repayment itself is the offense rather than the speed and exactness of it.

questions.stem: The author's comparison of paying a neighbor cash with bringing a pie serves primarily to

options.A: show that treating a favor as a sale can undermine the relationship a gift would sustain.
options.B: prove that cash payment is always offensive between neighbors, whatever the circumstances or amount.
options.C: demonstrate that neighbors should never expect any payment for help, however large the favor is.
options.D: show that pies are more valuable than cash because they require effort and personal attention.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author says the cash treats the neighbor as a vendor. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says 'may seem' faintly offensive, not always. C) The point is about relationship, not obligation to pay. D) The author says the cash may be worth more.
questions.trap: Over-generalizing a hedged illustration ('may seem') into an absolute rule.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the standard economic treatment of gifts is best described as

options.A: critical, regarding it as explaining the phenomenon away instead of explaining it.
options.B: indifferent, offering no evaluation of whether the standard economic treatment is adequate or not.
options.C: bitter, regarding it as dishonest and as a deliberate attempt to deceive readers about generosity.
options.D: supportive, regarding it as largely adequate for explaining why people give and receive gifts.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author says both standard responses miss what gift exchange is for. Why the others are wrong: B) The author evaluates it directly. C) The criticism is analytical, not accusatory. D) The author sides with the anthropologists.
questions.trap: Mistaking a measured criticism for hostility.

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the claim that deferred, unspecified return is essential to the way gifts bind people?

options.A: In some societies chiefs use lavish gifts to dominate rivals and secure the loyalty of their followers.
options.B: People who receive gifts report feeling obligated to the giver and uneasy until they have reciprocated.
options.C: Societies that require immediate, exact repayment sustain relationships as durable as societies with open-ended debts.
options.D: Merchants who give small favors to regular customers retain those customers longer than other merchants do.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) This shows durable bonds without open-ended obligation. Why the others are wrong: A) The author already accepts this and it does not test the claim. B) This is consistent with the claim. D) This supports the claim that gift-like favors bind.
questions.trap: Choosing a finding that the author already incorporates into the argument.

questions.stem: A company gives employees a bonus described as payment for meeting a quarterly target and also calls it a 'gift of appreciation.' Based on the passage, the author would predict that

options.A: employees will view the bonus as an insult because it is too large for the work done and implies a debt.
options.B: employees will feel stronger loyalty to the company because the bonus is generous and described as a gift.
options.C: employees will feel the bonus creates an open-ended obligation to the company that they must someday repay.
options.D: employees will recognize the calculated inducement, and the gift element will lose its force.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The final sentence says an explicit inducement loses its gift force. Why the others are wrong: A) Size is not the issue in the passage. B) The passage says explicit pricing weakens the relationship offered. C) An explicit target makes it payment, which closes the account.
questions.trap: Assuming that calling something a gift is enough to make it function as one.

passages.passage_text:
Satire is often defended on the ground that it reforms its targets: by exposing folly to ridicule, the satirist shames people into abandoning it. The defense has a long pedigree among satirists themselves, who have routinely announced reform as their purpose. But the historical record offers little evidence that ridiculed vices diminish under ridicule, and the persistence of the very follies that satirists lampooned centuries ago suggests that something other than correction is at work.

An alternative account locates the function of satire not in its effect on its targets but in its effect on its audience. A satirical piece addresses readers who already share the satirist's judgments and invites them to enjoy the confirmation of those judgments. The pleasure is the pleasure of recognition: the reader laughs because the portrait of the pompous official or the grasping merchant matches an opinion already held. Satire, on this view, does not change minds but consolidates communities, drawing a line between the knowing, who see the joke, and the targets, who do not. A joke that required explanation would fail in just the place where it was meant to succeed.

This account explains several features that the reform theory struggles with. It explains why satire so seldom troubles its targets, who typically are not reading. It explains why the most effective satire is often the most local, depending on allusions that outsiders cannot follow, and why it ages poorly once the allusions are lost. And it explains why satirists in every age have been more popular with those who agree with them than with those they attack, a pattern that would be puzzling if the aim were to persuade the unconverted. Each of these features follows naturally from the community account, whereas the reform account must treat all of them as unfortunate accidents of circumstance.

Yet the community-building theory has its own difficulties. If satire merely confirmed existing opinion, it would be hard to explain why authorities have so frequently feared it, censoring satirists, jailing them, or banning their plays. Rulers are not generally alarmed by entertainments that leave their opponents' views unchanged. The fear suggests that satire does something more than flatter an audience, and one plausible candidate is that it makes dissent publicly speakable. A grievance that individuals harbor privately gains a different status when it is voiced aloud and met with laughter, for the laughter shows each listener that others share the grievance. The effect is not to convert but to coordinate: to turn scattered private opinions into common knowledge.

If this is right, then both traditional and revisionist accounts have captured part of the truth. Satire does not reform its targets, as the defenders claim, but neither is it merely a form of self-congratulation, as the revisionists imply. Its power lies in the space between private opinion and public expression, a space in which a society decides what it is willing to say about itself. That satirists' own stated intentions may be mistaken about this need not surprise us; writers are rarely the best theorists of what their work accomplishes.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Satire's power lies less in reforming targets than in making private grievances publicly speakable and so coordinating audiences.
options.B: Satire merely flatters like-minded audiences and should not be taken seriously as a force in politics or culture.
options.C: Authorities fear satire because it persuades their own supporters to change sides and withdraw their loyalty.
options.D: Satire succeeds mainly by shaming its targets into reforming their conduct once their faults have been exposed.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) This is the final synthesis of the passage. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says the revisionists also capture only part of the truth. C) The passage does not claim this. D) The author rejects this claim.
questions.trap: Stopping at the revisionist account and missing the author's final coordination hypothesis.

questions.stem: According to the passage, satire tends to age poorly because

options.A: censors successfully suppress it before later generations have a chance to read it.
options.B: its targets eventually reform, which makes the satire irrelevant to readers of later periods.
options.C: its audience's opinions change over time, so the satirist's positions seem foreign to later readers.
options.D: its effectiveness depends on allusions that later readers cannot follow.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The third paragraph states this. Why the others are wrong: A) Censorship is raised for a different purpose. B) The author denies that targets reform. C) This is not stated.
questions.trap: Picking a plausible cause that the passage does not give.

questions.stem: The discussion of authorities censoring satirists serves to

options.A: prove that satire succeeds in reforming its targets, since authorities would not censor harmless writing.
options.B: celebrate the courage of satirists who risked prison and exile to criticize the powerful.
options.C: present a difficulty for the community-building account that motivates a further hypothesis
options.D: support the claim that satire seldom troubles its targets or the officials who govern them.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author says the fear suggests satire does more than flatter. Why the others are wrong: A) The author never concludes this. B) No such praise is offered. D) It does the opposite by suggesting rulers are troubled.
questions.trap: Reading the example as support for the account it actually challenges.

questions.stem: Which finding would most strengthen the author's final hypothesis about satire?

options.A: Satirists report that they intend to reform their targets and that they judge their success by whether reforms follow.
options.B: After a satirical play, audience members report greater willingness to discuss the targeted grievance openly.
options.C: Targets of satire rarely attend the performances, and those who do attend are rarely moved to change their conduct.
options.D: Satirical works from past centuries remain widely read, and modern readers still recognize most of the figures they mock.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) This shows satire making dissent publicly speakable. Why the others are wrong: A) The author treats stated intentions as unreliable. C) This fits the earlier claim but not the coordination hypothesis. D) This does not bear on public expression of grievances.
questions.trap: Choosing a finding consistent with an earlier claim rather than the specific hypothesis being tested.

questions.stem: The final sentence of the passage implies that satirists' stated intentions are

options.A: the best available evidence of what satire does and why it affects its audiences.
options.B: usually deliberately dishonest, since satirists wish to hide their real political aims.
options.C: irrelevant to literary study, which should consider only the text and its reception.
options.D: not a reliable guide to what their work accomplishes.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author says writers are rarely the best theorists of their work. Why the others are wrong: A) This is the opposite of the author's point. B) The author attributes error, not dishonesty. C) The author does not say intentions have no value, only that they are an unreliable guide.
questions.trap: Reading 'mistaken' as 'dishonest.'

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the passage's claim that satire seldom reforms its targets?

options.A: Rulers have often censored satirists and burned their works, sometimes imprisoning the authors for years.
options.B: Satire depends on local allusions that readers in other places or periods are unlikely to recognize.
options.C: Documented cases in which many satirized officials changed their conduct after reading the satire.
options.D: Many satirical works are read mainly by people who already share the satirist's views and attitudes.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) This is direct evidence of reform. Why the others are wrong: A) The author uses this for a different point and it does not show reform. B) This is part of the author's own account. D) This is consistent with the passage.
questions.trap: Choosing a fact the author already cites as consistent with the argument.

passages.passage_text:
When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The aphorism is cited so often that its force has dulled, but the phenomenon it describes is real and its mechanisms deserve closer attention than the slogan suggests. Consider a school system that wishes to know whether its students are learning to read. It administers a standardized test, and scores on the test are, at first, reasonably good indicators of reading ability: students who read well tend to score well, and the correlation is strong enough to be useful. Then the system attaches consequences to the scores. Schools whose scores rise receive funding; those whose scores fall are sanctioned. The correlation between scores and ability begins to weaken, not because the test has changed but because everyone involved has begun to respond to it.

The responses take several forms. The least troubling is straightforward improvement: teachers examine the test, identify the skills it measures, and teach those skills more effectively. If the test measures reading comprehension and teachers improve comprehension instruction, the system has achieved what it hoped. But the test samples only a portion of what reading involves, and teachers under pressure have reason to concentrate on that portion. Time spent on extended writing, on sustained engagement with long books, or on discussion of ambiguous texts, none of which the test captures, may shrink. Scores may rise while the broader ability they were meant to indicate stagnates. At the far end lie practices that involve no improvement at all, such as the strategic exclusion of weak students from testing or, in documented cases, outright alteration of answer sheets.

It is tempting to treat these responses as moral failures by individuals, but this diagnosis is too convenient. Teachers who narrow the curriculum are responding rationally to the incentives they have been given. If their institution rewards a number, they will produce the number; to expect otherwise is to expect them to sacrifice their schools in the name of a purity that no one has asked of the administrators who designed the system. The failing, if there is one, belongs largely to the design.

Does this mean that measurement should be abandoned? That conclusion would be too hasty. Without measurement, resources are allocated by anecdote and influence, and the students least able to advocate for themselves are the most likely to be overlooked. The more constructive conclusion is that measures are most reliable when they are not the sole basis for consequences, when several different indicators are consulted, and when the indicators are periodically changed so that effort cannot be fixed on a single target. Even these safeguards will not eliminate distortion, but they can reduce the degree to which a measure's usefulness is destroyed by the very attention that makes it matter.

The deeper lesson is that every measure is a proxy, and the gap between proxy and purpose is where gaming takes place. The wider that gap, and the higher the stakes attached to the proxy, the greater the opportunity and the incentive to exploit it.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Teachers who narrow the curriculum in order to raise scores should be disciplined for gaming the tests, since their conduct harms students.
options.B: Attaching high stakes to a measure tends to degrade its value as an indicator, but the remedy is better measurement, not abandonment.
options.C: Test scores never correlate with reading ability, which is why they should not be used to judge schools.
options.D: Standardized tests should be abandoned because they cannot capture what reading ability actually involves.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) This covers both the problem and the recommendation. Why the others are wrong: A) The author calls this diagnosis too convenient. C) The passage says they correlate at first. D) The author calls that conclusion too hasty.
questions.trap: Choosing the blame-the-teachers or abandon-the-test reading the author explicitly rejects.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the correlation between test scores and reading ability weakens after consequences are attached because

options.A: students stop reading outside school because test preparation takes up their free time.
options.B: schools and teachers begin to respond to the test itself.
options.C: the test becomes harder to pass as officials raise the passing standard each year.
options.D: the test is revised to include new skills that are less closely tied to reading ability.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author says everyone involved begins to respond to it. Why the others are wrong: A) This is not mentioned. C) The author says the test has not changed. D) The author says the test has not changed.
questions.trap: Missing the explicit statement that the test itself did not change.

questions.stem: The author discusses teachers improving comprehension instruction in order to

options.A: show that responding to a target is not always harmful.
options.B: argue that the test measures all of what reading involves.
options.C: claim that teachers are the main source of distortion.
options.D: show that test tampering is rare.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author calls this the least troubling response, one that achieves what the system hoped. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says it samples only a portion. C) The author locates the failing largely in design. D) No rate of tampering is given.
questions.trap: Treating a benign example as evidence for a claim about the test's completeness.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward teachers who narrow the curriculum is best described as

options.A: approving, regarding narrowing as good teaching because it focuses effort on what is measured.
options.B: understanding, locating the fault chiefly in the system's design.
options.C: detached, offering no view of where responsibility for the narrowing of the curriculum lies.
options.D: condemnatory, treating them as morally culpable for harming students to raise their own ratings.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author says they respond rationally to the incentives given. Why the others are wrong: A) The author notes the broader ability may stagnate. C) The author clearly assigns responsibility to design. D) The author calls that diagnosis too convenient.
questions.trap: Treating an explanation of behavior as approval of it.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best illustration of the 'gap between proxy and purpose' described in the final paragraph?

options.A: A city stops measuring crime rates altogether after officials conclude that police statistics cannot be trusted.
options.B: A company tracks sales using several different indicators so that no single figure can be manipulated.
options.C: A hospital is judged on surgical survival rates, and surgeons decline to operate on the sickest patients.
options.D: A school improves comprehension instruction after examining the test and then sees both scores and ability rise.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The proxy (survival rate) improves while the purpose (caring for patients) is undermined. Why the others are wrong: A) This abandons measurement, which the author does not recommend. B) This is a safeguard, not an exploitation of the gap. D) This improves the purpose along with the proxy.
questions.trap: Choosing an example about measurement in general rather than one in which the proxy is exploited.

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the author's suggestion that consulting several indicators and rotating them reduces distortion?

options.A: Schools quickly learn to raise every indicator in the rotation through the same narrow teaching practices.
options.B: Schools rarely exclude weak students from testing when several indicators are used, even when their ratings are at stake.
options.C: Test scores are somewhat correlated with other indicators of reading ability, such as grades and teacher evaluations.
options.D: Indicators that are never changed are gamed more heavily over time than indicators that are rotated regularly.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) This shows the safeguards do not reduce gaming. Why the others are wrong: B) This supports the suggestion. C) Correlation does not show that safeguards fail. D) This supports the suggestion.
questions.trap: Selecting a finding that sounds critical of testing but actually supports the author's recommendation.

passages.passage_text:
In the late twentieth century, the cleaning of several celebrated paintings provoked a controversy that revealed how little agreement exists about what a restorer is trying to restore. Conservators removed layers of aged varnish and grime, and the canvases emerged startlingly bright, their blues and reds more vivid than viewers had known. Admirers rejoiced that the artists' true colors had been recovered. Critics protested that the cleaning had stripped away subtle glazes, flattened the shadows, and produced a clarity the artists never intended.

Both sides assumed there was a determinate answer to the question of how the painting "really" looked. The admirers equated the original with the state of the painting at the moment it was finished; the critics equated it with the painting as it had come to be known and, in some cases, as the artist might have anticipated it would mature. Neither assumption is silly. Painters of earlier centuries knew that their pigments would darken and that varnish would yellow, and some applied final glazes expecting the surface to settle into a particular harmony. To remove everything added by time may therefore be to remove part of the work as its maker conceived it. At the same time, to leave a painting dimmed beneath layers that obscure its drawing and color is to deny viewers access to what the maker actually put on the canvas.

The dispute is complicated by the fact that the physical evidence is ambiguous. A conservator can distinguish original paint from later varnish under magnification and chemical analysis, but cannot always determine whether a thin, translucent layer was part of the artist's design or a later addition. In such cases the decision rests on judgment about the artist's intentions, and those intentions must be inferred from the work itself, from fragments of documentary evidence, and from comparison with other paintings, each a source of uncertainty. A restorer who claims to be merely uncovering the truth is concealing the interpretive character of the act.

This suggests that the controversy is less about technique than about what we value in old pictures. Those who prize authenticity of materials will favor minimal intervention, preferring a painting that shows its age honestly to one that has been made to look new. Those who prize the visual experience the artist designed will favor more aggressive cleaning, accepting some risk of loss for the sake of legibility. These priorities are not reducible to facts about the paint; they are commitments, and reasonable people can hold either. A restorer's decision about how far to clean is therefore a decision about which of these goods to sacrifice, and no measurement of the paint can make that decision on the restorer's behalf.

The best practice, accordingly, is probably neither bold nor timid but transparent. Restorers should document each stage of treatment, retain samples of removed material when possible, and avoid permanent measures that foreclose later reconsideration. Because the judgments embodied in any restoration will in time look as dated as the varnish they replaced, the most valuable thing a conservator can leave is the means by which a future generation can undo them.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Aggressive cleaning is justified because it recovers the artist's true colors, which later varnish and grime have hidden for centuries.
options.B: Restoration disputes arise because restoring involves interpretive judgments and competing values, so transparent, reversible treatment is best.
options.C: The critics of the cleaning were correct and the admirers mistaken, since the cleaned surface lacks the harmony the artist intended.
options.D: Minimal intervention is always the best policy for old paintings, since any removal of material permanently destroys evidence of the artist's intentions and the work's history.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) This covers the cause of the dispute and the recommendation. Why the others are wrong: A) The author calls this one of two assumptions that are not determinate. C) The author says neither assumption is silly. D) The author says both priorities are legitimate commitments.
questions.trap: Siding with one party in the controversy when the author declines to.

questions.stem: The author claims physical evidence cannot settle restoration disputes because

options.A: documentary evidence about artists' intentions is almost always absent from the historical record altogether.
options.B: chemical analysis cannot distinguish paint from varnish at all, even with modern instruments and samples.
options.C: painters of earlier centuries disagreed about the use of varnish, so no single practice can be assumed.
options.D: conservators cannot always tell whether a thin translucent layer was part of the artist's design.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author says this directly in the third paragraph. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says it exists in fragments. B) The author says conservators can usually distinguish them. C) No such disagreement is mentioned.
questions.trap: Overstating the ambiguity into an inability to distinguish any layers.

questions.stem: The statement that painters knew pigments would darken and varnish would yellow serves to

options.A: suggest that earlier painters were careless about durability.
options.B: prove that artists wanted their paintings to appear dark.
options.C: argue that restorers have misled the public.
options.D: show that the critics' position has a reasonable basis.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) It supports the idea that aged surfaces can be part of the work as conceived. Why the others are wrong: A) They are described as aware and planning for aging. B) The passage says only that some expected a harmony to settle. C) The author does not say this.
questions.trap: Over-reading a supporting detail as proof of a stronger claim.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward a restorer who claims merely to be uncovering the truth is best described as

options.A: skeptical, because the claim hides the interpretive nature of the work.
options.B: hostile, accusing the restorer of fraud and of deliberately misleading museum visitors.
options.C: admiring of the restorer's confidence in being able to recover the original surface.
options.D: indifferent to what restorers claim, since claims have no bearing on how paintings are treated.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author says it conceals the interpretive character of the act. Why the others are wrong: B) The author describes concealment of interpretation, not fraud. C) The author criticizes the claim. D) The author takes a clear position.
questions.trap: Escalating a methodological criticism into an accusation of dishonesty.

questions.stem: A museum is choosing between two plans for a darkened painting. Plan X removes all later layers permanently. Plan Y removes only clearly later grime, documents each step, keeps samples, and uses reversible methods. The author would most likely favor

options.A: neither plan, because any intervention falsifies the work and any restoration is a fabrication.
options.B: Plan X, because it uncovers the painting as the artist finished it and removes every later addition.
options.C: Plan Y, because it guarantees that the original appearance will be recovered and later critics will agree.
options.D: Plan Y, because it preserves the means for future generations to reconsider today's judgments.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author recommends documentation and avoiding permanent measures. Why the others are wrong: A) The author does not oppose all intervention. B) The author says this is an assumption, not a settled fact. C) The author says no treatment guarantees that.
questions.trap: Choosing the right plan for the wrong reason, such as a guarantee of authenticity the author denies exists.
